html:
Coltan, an ore of the metal tantalum used in phones and computers, became a symbol of conflict minerals when its price soared in 2000 and armed groups in the eastern Congo seized mines to sell it.

Much of it is dug by hand by miners, including children, in unsafe pits. During the Second Congo War and the Kivu conflict, armies and rebels taxed and smuggled it, with much passing through Rwanda.

A United States law of 2010 required firms to check whether minerals came from conflict zones, and many began audits. The Congo is also the source of most of the world's cobalt, vital for batteries in electric cars, from the same southern copper belt once run by Gécamines.
sum: Coltan, an ore of the metal tantalum used in phones and computers, became a symbol of conflict minerals when its price soared in 2000 and armed groups in the eastern Congo seized mines to sell it.
